draft.title: Vector projections
card: The vector projection of a onto b is the part of a that points along b. It is a vector in the direction of b (or the opposite direction).
Scalar projection
a·b ÷ |b|. This is a signed length. It is negative when the angle between a and b is obtuse.
Vector projection
(a·b ÷ |b|²) b. This is the scalar projection multiplied by the unit vector in the direction of b.
Example: a = 3i + 4j and b = 2i. Then a·b = 6 and |b|² = 4, so the vector projection is (6 ÷ 4)(2i) = 3i.
draft.remember: Projection of a onto b: find a·b, divide by |b|², then multiply b by the result.

a.q: Let a = 2i + 5j and b = 3i. What is the vector projection of a onto b?
a.why: a·b = 6 and |b|² = 9, so the projection is (6 ÷ 9)(3i) = 2i. This is the part of a along the i direction. 6i is the scalar product times b divided by nothing, so it skips the division by |b|².
a.clue: Find a·b and |b|² first, then scale b.

b.q: Mia walks with displacement a = 4i + 3j. A road runs in the direction of b = 3i − 4j. What is the scalar projection of a onto b?
b.why: a·b = 4×3 + 3×(−4) = 0, and |b| = 5, so the scalar projection is 0 ÷ 5 = 0. The vectors are perpendicular, so none of a lies along b. The option 5 is |a| or |b|, not the projection.
b.clue: Work out a·b first. What does its value tell you about the angle?

problems.detail: The why says 6i is 'the scalar product times b divided by nothing'. That is wrong: (a·b)b = 6 × 3i = 18i. 6i comes from dividing by |b| instead of |b|² ((6 ÷ 3)(3i)), or from multiplying a·b by the unit vector i.

The card says the vector projection is a vector in the direction of b or the opposite direction. It leaves out the case where a is perpendicular to b and the projection is the zero vector, which is exactly the case in question b.

check.summary: Both questions and their intended answers (2i and 0) are correct. The explanation for question a gives a wrong account of where the 6i distractor comes from. The card also leaves out the zero-projection case when the vectors are perpendicular, which question b uses.

final.title: Vector projections
card: The vector projection of \(a\) onto \(b\) is the part of \(a\) that points along \(b\). It points in the direction of \(b\) or the opposite direction, or it is the zero vector when \(a\) is perpendicular to \(b\).
Scalar projection
\(a \cdot b \div |b|\). This is a signed length. It is negative when the angle between \(a\) and \(b\) is obtuse, and 0 when they are perpendicular.
Vector projection
\(\left(a \cdot b \div |b|^{2}\right) b\). This is the scalar projection multiplied by the unit vector in the direction of \(b\).
Example: \(a = 3i + 4j\) and \(b = 2i\). Then \(a \cdot b = 6\) and \(|b|^{2} = 4\), so the vector projection is \((6 \div 4)(2i) = 3i\).
final.remember: Projection of \(a\) onto \(b\): find \(a \cdot b\), divide by \(|b|^{2}\), then multiply \(b\) by the result.

a.q: Let \(a = 2i + 5j\) and \(b = 3i\). What is the vector projection of \(a\) onto \(b\)?
a.why: \(a \cdot b = 6\) and \(|b|^{2} = 9\), so the projection is \((6 \div 9)(3i) = 2i\). This is the part of \(a\) along the \(i\) direction. \(6i\) comes from dividing by \(|b|\) instead of \(|b|^{2}\), giving \((6 \div 3)(3i)\), or from multiplying \(a \cdot b\) by the unit vector \(i\).
a.clue: Find \(a \cdot b\) and \(|b|^{2}\) first, then scale \(b\).

b.q: Mia walks with displacement \(a = 4i + 3j\). A road runs in the direction of \(b = 3i - 4j\). What is the scalar projection of \(a\) onto \(b\)?
b.why: \(a \cdot b = 4 \times 3 + 3 \times (-4) = 0\), and \(|b| = 5\), so the scalar projection is \(0 \div 5 = 0\). The vectors are perpendicular, so none of \(a\) lies along \(b\). The option 5 is \(|a|\) or \(|b|\), not the projection.
b.clue: Work out \(a \cdot b\) first. What does its value tell you about the angle?
